planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Crosby's Compact stays smaller and denser than standard jade and rarely needs repotting into large containers.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix, watering only after the soil dries out completely. Crosby's Compact is a dwarf jade plant cultivar distinguished by small, tightly cupped, rounded leaves that curl slightly inward, giving the foliage a denser, more crowded texture than the flat-leaved standard jade plant. Its slow, compact growth habit makes it a popular choice for small containers, dish gardens, and succulent bonsai, since it rarely needs the aggressive pruning larger jade cultivars require to stay tidy. Leaf margins take on a reddish blush in strong light, and like other jade plants it propagates readily from leaf or stem cuttings.
sources: World of Succulents — Crassula ovata cultivar guide

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Botany Bay colors up best with strong light and infrequent watering.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix, letting the soil dry out fully between waterings. Botany Bay is a compact jade plant cultivar prized for its dense, low-mounding habit and small, rounded, glossy leaves that develop pronounced bright red margins when grown in strong sun, contrasting sharply with the green leaf centers. It forms a tidier, shrubbier plant than the standard jade plant and is popular for succulent dish gardens and bonsai-style specimens. As with other jade plant cultivars, it is easy to propagate from leaf or stem cuttings and tolerates the low humidity typical of indoor growing conditions.
sources: World of Succulents — Crassula ovata cultivar guide
Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Direct sow outdoors after danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; like its Double Click series-mates, Snow Puff takes a bit longer than single-flowered cosmos to reach its first flush of bloom.

directions: Double Click Snow Puff produces fully double, ruffled pure-white blooms on the same tall, wiry stems as the rest of the Double Click line, giving a pompom-like, dahlia-style flower instead of the flat single daisy typical of Cosmos bipinnatus. It pairs well as a cut-flower companion to the Cranberry and Rose Bonbon shades in the series, offering a clean white accent for mixed bouquets. Like other Double Click colors, it flowers later than single-type cosmos but blooms continuously from midsummer through frost once established, and it thrives in lean, well-drained soil with only moderate watering. Frequent cutting encourages continued branching and bloom production.
sources: PanAmerican Seed — Double Click Cosmos Series
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Cosmos Variety Listings

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early for earlier bloom; thin seedlings once established.

directions: Apricot Lemonade produces single, flat daisy-form blooms in a soft blend of warm apricot, peach, cream, and buttery yellow tones, each flower shading subtly from petal base to tip for a painterly, watercolor effect. The airy, fern-like foliage and tall, branching habit make it a favorite for cottage-style borders and cutting gardens alike, and its unusual warm color range fills a niche among the more common pink, white, and crimson bipinnatus shades. Like other cosmos, it flowers best in lean, well-drained soil and struggles in overly rich beds where foliage outpaces bloom. Regular deadheading or cutting for bouquets keeps plants flowering from summer until the first hard frost.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cosmic Yellow is a compact, early-flowering selection that tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil better than most bedding annuals.

directions: Cosmic Yellow is a dwarf, mounding selection of Cosmos sulphureus bred as a companion shade to Cosmic Orange, bearing bright golden-yellow single blooms above finely cut, dark green foliage on compact 12-18 inch plants. Its low, tidy habit suits front-of-border plantings, containers, and mass bedding where taller cosmos would flop or overwhelm. It begins flowering earlier than standard-sized sulphureus types and continues nonstop through summer heat into fall with no deadheading required. Like other Cosmic series selections, it is highly heat- and drought-tolerant once established and performs poorly in rich, heavily fertilized soil.

common_name: Cerro Potosi Baby Sage (True Cherry-Red Salvia)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or set out container plants in spring, in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; this selection was originally collected on Cerro Potosi in Nuevo Leon, Mexico, and is prized for flowers of true, saturated cherry-red rather than the pink or bicolor tones common in the species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates. Cerro Potosi forms a compact, woody-based mound of small aromatic leaves topped from late spring through frost with dense racemes of pure cherry-red, two-lipped flowers that are a magnet for hummingbirds. Cut back hard to 6-12 inches in late winter to renew growth and maintain a tidy shape, and expect vigorous rebloom through the following season. Once established it tolerates heat and drought with ease, needing supplemental water only during extended dry spells.

common_name: Frieda Dixon Pineapple Sage (Salmon-Flowered Pineapple Sage)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants after all danger of frost has passed, in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this cultivar is grown for its unusual soft salmon-pink flower spikes, a departure from the scarlet-red blooms of the straight species.

directions: Grow in fertile, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot summer climates; strong midday sun can stress the foliage. Frieda Dixon produces the same pineapple-scented, edible leaves as the species but bears loose spikes of soft salmon-pink tubular flowers in fall rather than the typical bright red, making it a favorite for gardeners wanting a softer color echo in late-season borders. Pinch young growth through summer to encourage bushiness and delay flowering slightly, and mulch the crown over winter in zone 8 since top growth is usually killed back by frost even though the roots survive. Flowers are a strong late-season hummingbird draw.

common_name: King George Hens and Chicks (Cilia-Fringed Russet Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: King George is a Hansen-bred sempervivum with narrow, upright leaves fringed in fine white cilia that shift between russet-red and green through the growing season. It offsets freely, quickly building dense mounded clusters of tight rosettes around each parent plant. Full sun sharpens the seasonal color change and keeps rosettes compact, while afternoon shade helps where summers run consistently above 80F. As with all hen-and-chicks types, sharply drained mineral soil is essential to prevent crown rot over winter.

common_name: Red Rubin Hens and Chicks (Goos and Koenemann Bicolor Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Red Rubin, a Goos and Koenemann introduction, carries a glowing red center that fades outward into silvery-green leaf tips, then flushes fully burgundy across the whole rosette once cold weather sets in. It is a reliable offsetter, filling in troughs and crevice plantings with tight, cilia-edged rosettes within a season or two. Give it full sun for the sharpest color contrast and keep the crown dry, since standing water after heavy rain is its main cause of failure. This bicolor patterning distinguishes it from the solid ruby-toned 'Rubin' already common in cultivation.

common_name: Cherry Frost Hens and Chicks (Payne Cobwebbed Maroon Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Cherry Frost, a Payne cultivar, pairs maroon and jade coloring with long, curling cilia along the leaf margins and tips that give each rosette a dew-dusted look year-round. It offsets steadily via short stolons, forming dense clusters that read as a single frosted mound within a couple of seasons. Full sun keeps the cilia prominent and the color saturated, while light afternoon shade prevents scorch during extended heat. Keep it on the dry side between waterings, since the same fine hairs that give it its frosted texture also trap moisture against the crown if soil stays wet.

common_name: Pixie Hens and Chicks (Nixon Miniature Cobweb Sempervivum)

planting.note: Tuck offsets into shallow pockets of very well-drained, lean, gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Pixie is a Nixon-bred selection of Sempervivum arachnoideum, the cobweb houseleek, producing unusually small, tight green rosettes only a couple of inches across that pick up pink to red edging in strong light. Fine webbing across each rosette tip gives it the same cobwebbed look as the species, just in miniature. It cascades nicely over rock edges and between paver joints, producing abundant offsets that knit into a dense, low mat. Because the rosettes are so small, plant it where it won't be overrun by larger companion sempervivums.

common_name: Moss Rose Hens and Chicks (Green and Pink Cilia-Edged Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Moss Rose forms a fuller, larger rosette than many sempervivum cultivars, packed with pointed green and pink leaves edged in long cilia. Despite the common name, it is unrelated to Portulaca moss rose — this is a true hen-and-chicks type that offsets heavily each spring, sending up pink flower stalks on mature rosettes. Full sun is needed to keep the pink tones from washing out to plain green. Grow it in gritty, sharply drained soil and hold back on water once cooler fall weather sets in.

common_name: Saturn Hens and Chicks (Skrocki Velvety Red-Green Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Saturn, a Skrocki hybrid, has a velvety-textured rosette that mixes red and green tones through most of the year before deepening to solid burgundy in winter. It is a strong offsetter, filling gravel beds and troughs with clustered rosettes within a season or two of planting. Full sun brings out the deepest winter color and keeps the fine leaf hairs from matting in humid weather. Like other hardy sempervivums it goes dormant and shrinks slightly in winter, then rebounds with new growth and fresh offsets in spring.

common_name: Karola Hens and Chicks (Smits Purple-Tipped Velvet Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Karola, bred by Smits, has a soft, velvety rosette covered in fine short hairs, with an apple-green base contrasting against purple-tipped leaves. It sends offsets out on noticeably long runners, making it well suited to cascading over the edges of pots and raised beds rather than staying in a tight clump. Full sun brings out the strongest purple tipping; in shade the tips fade toward plain green. Grow it in sharply drained, mineral soil and avoid overhead watering that can pool in the rosette center.

common_name: Gazelle Hens and Chicks (Ford Red-Yellow-Green Striped Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Gazelle, a Ford introduction, carries long, fuzzy leaves with unusual striping in red, yellow, and green, edged in fine white cilia that catch the light. It offsets reliably, producing new rosettes around the base of each parent plant through the growing season. Full sun is essential to hold the striped pattern; without it the leaves tend toward plain green. As with other hardy sempervivums, sharply drained gravelly soil and protection from standing water are key to keeping the crown from rotting.

common_name: Spring Beauty Hens and Chicks (Cobweb-Tufted Pink-Blushed Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Spring Beauty has a sweet green rosette that picks up a soft pink blush along the outer leaves, with light cobweb-like tufting at each leaf tip. Color shifts further toward pink as temperatures drop in fall and winter, giving the clump seasonal interest beyond its usual green summer look. It offsets on stolons at a steady pace, filling gaps in crevice gardens and gravel beds within a season or two. Give it full to partial sun and well-draining, gritty soil, and keep it away from standing water that lingers after rain.

common_name: Maria Laach Hens and Chicks (von Stein-Zeppelin Purple-Brown Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Maria Laach, named for the German abbey and bred by von Stein-Zeppelin, forms a medium-to-large rosette combining deep purple and chestnut-brown outer leaves with a bright green interior. In winter the color deepens further until nearly the whole rosette turns purple. It is a generous offsetter, quickly forming substantial clumps in rock gardens and troughs. Full to partial sun keeps the contrast between the dark outer leaves and green center sharp, and, as with all sempervivums, sharply drained soil is essential to prevent rot.

common_name: Reinhardt Hens and Chicks (Haberer Award-Winning Green-Black Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Reinhardt, bred by Haberer, is a vigorous grower with apple-green centers giving way to near-black tips on long, narrow, upright leaves — a combination that earned it the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit in 2008. It builds into sizeable clumps over time as offsets fill in around each rosette. Full sun brings out the darkest tip color and keeps growth compact; in shade the rosettes loosen and stretch. Plant in sharply drained, lean soil and shield the crown from prolonged wet spells.

common_name: Harlequin Rouge Hens and Chicks (Jensen and Elliott Large Gold-Red Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Harlequin Rouge, from breeders Jensen and Elliott, is one of the larger sempervivum cultivars, with long, sturdy leaves that shift between lush green and sunny gold and red tones through the seasons. It offsets on stolons and, given its size, needs more room than typical hen-and-chicks types to show off its full rosette form. Full to partial sun with afternoon shade in hot climates keeps the color transitions vivid. As with other hardy sempervivums, gritty, sharply drained soil is critical, since this larger rosette can hold moisture longer than smaller cultivars and is more prone to rot if kept wet.
